suggestion: Obtain a lawful, timestamped closing-line source before building anything else.
why: Every decision the project cares about — edge, ROI, ATS accuracy, parlay value, leaderboard scoring — requires the price that was actually available. Without it we can only measure prediction accuracy, which is not the same thing as profitability.
cost: Licensing cost and legal review; feeds may not permit redistribution, which would limit what can be published.
acceptance: For each game, a stored quote with source, market, line, price and capture time, and at least one full historical season to test on.

suggestion: Fix the measurement target: decide whether the leaderboard scores straight-up winners or spread performance.
why: They are different games. This dataset shows a ~60% straight-up hit rate that is statistically indistinguishable from luck, while spread performance cannot be computed at all yet. Scoring the wrong metric rewards the wrong strategies.
cost: None in money; requires a written pre-registration so the metric cannot be changed after results are known.
acceptance: A signed-off metric definition, the minimum sample, and the promotion threshold, all fixed before the next season's data arrives.

suggestion: Automate the weekly capture so the sample grows without hand entry, and re-run verification on every update.
why: The verdict on every strategy is currently limited by sample size (136 games). Automation converts each week into fresh out-of-sample evidence instead of one static snapshot.
cost: Engineering time; needs a permitted data channel because the current sandbox cannot reach the data host directly.
acceptance: A scheduled job that fetches, stores with timestamp and URL, re-runs the gate, and fails loudly if reconciliation breaks.

suggestion: Build the backup/attrition layer on participation snapshots, not depth charts.
why: Official NFL depth charts are not published, so '2nd string' cannot be sourced. Who actually played — snapped counts and participation — is the defensible proxy for a starter being replaced.
cost: Requires a row-level participation feed; no official free source was found in this environment.
acceptance: For each injured starter, a dated record of the replacement and that player's snap share, linked to a source.

suggestion: Pre-register a small number of hypotheses instead of testing many strategies.
why: Four strategies were tested here and the best result stopped being significant after correction. Testing fewer, pre-declared ideas is the cheapest way to make a real edge detectable.
cost: Slower iteration; fewer headline numbers to show.
acceptance: A written hypothesis list with direction and threshold fixed in advance, and results reported for all of them, including failures.

suggestion: Publish failures prominently, exactly as this site does.
why: The model failing its gate and the near-significant strategy are the two most decision-relevant facts produced. Hiding them would make the dashboard actively misleading.
cost: Counter-intuitive to market; requires discipline to keep showing.
acceptance: Every strategy page shows its gate status, sample size and confidence interval next to its result.

suggestion: Only after the above: paper leaderboard, then prizes with legal review.
why: Rewards create pressure to overfit and to game the metric. Running paper-only first tests both the strategies and the scoring rules at zero financial risk.
cost: Prize funding, eligibility and jurisdiction review, audit and anti-fraud controls, tax treatment.
acceptance: A full paper season, locked predictions, independent audit, published rules, and a legal opinion before any money moves.
